summary:
This evaluation covered 6 EKS node-join diagnostic chat tasks, 3 iterations each; 2 of the 6 evals (negative-trigger tests, "cost-report" and "already-joined-scaling") were correctly skipped because they are should_trigger:false cases, so no variant data applies there (both variants fired the "no diagnosis needed" trigger 3/3, which is a pass on the no-op expectation, not a quality signal). The remaining 4 evals form the substantive comparison, and the picture is mixed and generally weak for both variants rather than favoring one clearly.

Trigger firing: in nj-live-node-not-joining the diagnostic trigger only fired 2/3 runs (one run presumably didn't engage at all), and in nj-al2-on-133-knowledge it also fired 2/3; the other two evals triggered reliably (3/3 and 2/2).

Expected-output and assertion pass rates swing inconsistently between variants across evals, with no clean pattern:
- nj-live-node-not-joining: with_skill met expected output 1/3 (33%), without_skill 0/2 (0%); only with_skill has assertion-level data (7/10, 70%), without_skill's assertion data is entirely missing, so this eval can't be compared on assertions.
- nj-live-node-notready-diagnose: with_skill met expected output 3/3 (100%) vs without_skill 0/3 (0%) — a sizable gap — but assertion pass rates were closer (with_skill 7/12=58%, without_skill 2/4=50%). Within this eval, one assertion (correct joined-then-lost classification) passes for both variants always, one (naming the node-side SSM blind spot) fails for both variants always, and one (tying reasoning to NJ check IDs) is flaky for both. These shared pass/fail patterns mean those particular assertions aren't distinguishing the variants — the gap seen in "expected output" isn't fully explained by assertion-level behavior.
- nj-al2-on-133-knowledge: here the direction flips — with_skill met expected output 0/3 (0%) vs without_skill 1/2 (50%), and on assertions with_skill scored 0/4 (0%) vs without_skill 3/8 (38%). Notably one specific assertion (stating the precise AL2/1.33 AMI deprecation reason) passed for without_skill (2/2) and failed for with_skill (0/1) — a clear per-assertion divergence favoring without_skill here. Two other assertions (NJ22 attribution, Critical severity labeling) failed for both variants entirely, flagging those checks/behaviors as unmet regardless of variant.
- nj-aws-auth-path-knowledge: with_skill has no assertion data at all (null), so only without_skill can be assessed (expected output 2/3=67%, assertions 1/6=17%); no side-by-side comparison is possible for this eval.

Confidence levels on these expected-output and LLM-graded assertion judgments are mostly medium-to-high, but sample sizes are very small (often 1-3 runs per cell), so each percentage rests on very few observations and should be read as indicative rather than robust.

Quality comparison pairs: every eval shows 0 pairs evaluated and all pairs skipped for direct quality comparison, so no head-to-head quality judgment is available anywhere in this dataset.

Output consistency: only one eval (nj-live-node-notready-diagnose) produced a consistency score, and only for with_skill ("mostly_consistent", high confidence); without_skill and all other evals have no consistency data, so run-to-run stability is largely unmeasured for without_skill and for most evals.

Runtime and cost: with_skill and without_skill trade off across evals rather than one being consistently faster/cheaper — e.g., in nj-live-node-not-joining with_skill took ~1m5s/$0.54 vs without_skill's ~1s/$0.02 (a large gap, though without_skill's near-instant run coincides with its 0/2 expected-output pass rate there, suggesting it may not have done substantive work); in nj-al2-on-133-knowledge the pattern reverses, with with_skill at 13s/$0.11 vs without_skill at 1m43s/$0.86. In nj-live-node-notready-diagnose with_skill ran longer and cost more (1m34s/$0.79 vs 29s/$0.25) while also scoring higher on expected output. These runtime/cost differences do not line up in one consistent direction across evals, so they look like per-task tradeoffs rather than a systematic efficiency difference.

Overall: with 3 of 30 iterations failing outright, several null/missing assertion or consistency fields, zero evaluated quality-comparison pairs, and expected-output results that favor with_skill in one eval, without_skill in another, and are incomparable in a third, this is a thin and inconsistent dataset. No dimension shows a stable advantage for either variant across the evals, and several assertions that should distinguish diagnostic quality (e.g., NJ-check-ID attribution, severity labeling, the SSM blind-spot callout) failed for both variants wherever they could be checked — indicating a shared weakness in the underlying diagnostic skill behavior rather than a variant-specific issue.

nj-live-node-not-joining.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat-based incident-RCA scenario (EKS node-join diagnostics), and the data available is quite limited, so conclusions should be read cautiously.

Trigger/applicability: the behavior under test fired in 2 of 3 runs (67%), meaning one run didn't produce a comparable scenario at all - already reducing the sample size for everything downstream.

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in 1 of 3 runs (33%), with high confidence in that judgment. without_skill met the expected output in 0 of 2 runs (0%), though only 2 runs were judged for it (one fewer than with_skill) and no confidence rating is given beyond "0 low_confidence" flags. Both variants struggled to meet the expected output, with with_skill succeeding slightly more often, but the sample sizes (3 and 2 runs) are too small to treat this as a stable difference.

Assertions: Only with_skill has per-assertion data; without_skill has no assertion data at all (marked null throughout), so no side-by-side assertion comparison is possible for this eval. For with_skill, overall assertion pass rate was 7/10 (70%). Breaking it down: two assertions passed fully (severity labeling 2/2, and remediation steps ordered by severity 2/2); one was roughly a coin flip (NJ identifier labeling, 1/2); and two others also landed at 1/2 (report structured as per-check PASS/FAIL/SKIPPED diagnostic rather than free-form list, and scoping to the skill's defined node-join checks), both judged with only medium confidence by the LLM evaluator. The "pattern" field for every assertion is marked "inconclusive," signaling the evaluators themselves flag these as not clearly resolved one way or the other. Since without_skill has no assertion results, we cannot say whether these same checks would have passed, failed, or differed for it.

Metrics: with_skill took much longer and cost much more (runtime ~1m5s, cost ~$0.54) than without_skill (runtime ~1s, cost ~$0.02). Context window utilization was low for both (5.3% vs 3.8%) with no compaction events for either. This is a large runtime/cost gap, but on its own it doesn't indicate which output was more useful - it needs to be weighed against quality, and quality data here is not available (see below).

Quality comparison: no quality pairs could actually be evaluated (0 of 3 pairs_evaluated, all 3 skipped), so there is no direct quality comparison to report - this dimension is effectively silent for this eval.

Output consistency: both variants show null/no data for consistency across repeated runs, so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed for either variant.

Overall state: this eval provides partial, low-sample data. with_skill has assertion-level detail (mixed results, several at 50% with only medium confidence, and all marked "inconclusive") while without_skill has no assertion or quality data to compare against, only a lower expected-output pass rate on fewer judged runs and much lower runtime/cost. Because quality comparisons were entirely skipped and consistency data is absent for both, it is not possible to weigh the large runtime/cost gap against output quality with any confidence. The clearest finding is that this eval, as currently instrumented, yields too little comparable data (small samples, missing without_skill assertion/quality data, inconclusive assertion patterns) to support a confident judgment in either direction.

nj-live-node-notready-diagnose.summary:
This single chat-task eval (an EKS node incident RCA scenario) shows a clear split on one dimension and limited data elsewhere.

Trigger and expected output: The behavior under test fired in all 3 runs for both variants (3/3). However, "expected output" diverges sharply: with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (3/3, 100%), while without_skill met it in 0 of 3 runs (0%). Both measurements carry medium (not low) confidence, so this gap is a reasonably solid finding, though it rests on only 3 runs per variant.

Assertions: Note with_skill was evaluated against 12 assertion instances (3 runs x 4 assertions) while without_skill shows only 4 (apparently 1 run x 4 assertions) — so the assertion-level comparison is based on much thinner data for without_skill. Aggregate pass rates look similar (with_skill 58%, without_skill 50%), but looking at individual assertions tells a more nuanced story:
- One assertion (classifying the node as "joined-then-lost/unhealthy") passed 100% for both variants — this assertion doesn't differentiate them.
- One assertion (naming the node-side blind spot and pointing to the SSM-based diagnostics complement) failed for both variants (0%) — this suggests either the assertion or the underlying agent behavior needs attention regardless of variant.
- One assertion (not claiming a mutating/write operation) passed 100% for both — again not differentiating.
- One assertion (tying reasoning to specific NJ check identifiers) was flaky for with_skill (1/3, 33%) and failed for without_skill's single sample (0/1) — too little data on without_skill to draw a confident contrast here, though neither variant performed well on it.

Metrics: with_skill ran considerably longer (avg ~1m34s) and cost more (~$0.79) than without_skill (avg ~29s, ~$0.25) — roughly 3x the time and cost. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (6.4% vs 5.2%), with no compactions for either.

Quality comparison: No head-to-head quality pairs could actually be evaluated (0 of 3 pairs compared, all 3 skipped), so there is no quality-based signal to weigh alongside the other dimensions here.

Consistency: with_skill showed "mostly consistent" output across repeated runs (score 2.0, high confidence). No consistency data is available for without_skill (null), so we cannot compare run-to-run stability between the two.

Overall state: The most notable and best-supported difference is on expected-output match (with_skill passing all runs, without_skill passing none), though this is based on a small sample (3 runs) at medium confidence. Against that, with_skill took substantially longer and cost more than without_skill. Assertion-level data shows some behaviors (the blind-spot/complement check) failing for both variants and others passing for both, meaning those particular checks aren't distinguishing the variants or indicate shared gaps; the NJ-check-identifier assertion was weak for both but with very limited sample for without_skill. No quality-comparison data or without_skill consistency data exist to further weigh the tradeoff, so this should be read as a partial picture: a clear expected-output gap favoring with_skill's pass rate, offset by a runtime/cost advantage for without_skill, with several key comparison dimensions (quality pairs, consistency for without_skill) absent.

answer_consistency.reasoning: All three outputs reach the same core diagnosis: the EC2 instance (i-1234567890abcdef0_1) behind node ip-192-168-100-153 no longer exists (InvalidInstanceID.NotFound), the kubelet stopped posting status around Sep 29 20:05/20:06 UTC, the node is tainted unreachable, and the cloud-node-lifecycle-controller has been looping ~232,644 times over 13 days trying and failing to delete the stale Node object. This is a Karpenter-provisioned spot node, and RBAC blocked direct inspection of Karpenter CRDs in all three. However, iteration 3 adds a materially new and significant fact not present in iterations 1 and 2: that there is currently NO active compute management at all (no managed node group, no running ASG, no live Karpenter NodePool, EKS Auto Mode disabled) — implying the cluster has had no real compute for ~2 weeks, a much more severe framing. Iterations 1 and 2 treat this as 'Karpenter is likely unhealthy / stuck finalizer' rather than 'no compute management exists at all'. This is a material addition/divergence in iteration 3.

recommendation_consistency.reasoning: All three recommend deleting the stale Node object as the top priority action, and all three note they cannot execute the deletion themselves (or ask permission). All also recommend investigating/checking Karpenter health or logs as a secondary step. However, iteration 3 adds materially different additional recommendations: restoring compute capacity entirely (fix Karpenter, create managed node group, or enable EKS Auto Mode), auditing CloudTrail for who terminated the instance, and tightening a security group rule (10250 inbound). Iterations 1 and 2 focus more narrowly on checking Karpenter NodeClaim state and controller logs, and iteration 2 specifically suggests force-delete with --force flag and checks for pod rescheduling, which iteration 1 doesn't explicitly mention using --force. The primary recommendation (delete stale node) is consistent, but the additional steps diverge enough for mostly_consistent rather than full consistency.

format_consistency.reasoning: All three use a prose-plus-structured-list format with a root cause section, evidence/checklist, and numbered recommended actions. Iteration 2 uniquely includes two markdown tables (Checklist Results and an implicit evidence table), while iteration 1 includes one evidence table. Iteration 3 uses no tables at all, relying purely on bullet points and prose. This represents a difference in presentation choice (table vs. no table) across the three, placing them as recognizably the same shape but differing in a presentation element.

nj-al2-on-133-knowledge.summary:
This single chat eval (an EKS/AL2-on-1.33 incident-RCA style task) shows some data gaps and a notable difference on the dimensions that could be measured, but the sample sizes are very small (2-3 runs per variant), so confidence in any pattern is limited.

Trigger behavior: the behavior under test fired in 2/3 runs overall (67%), meaning for at least one run the scenario didn't engage as expected, which already shrinks the usable sample.

Expected output: without_skill met the expected output in 1 of 2 evaluated runs (50%, medium confidence), while with_skill met it in 0 of 3 runs (0%, high confidence). Both are small samples, but without_skill's result rests on medium-confidence judgments, which somewhat weakens how much weight to put on its single pass.

Assertions: without_skill passed 3/8 assertion checks (38%) vs with_skill's 0/4 (0%). Breaking this down by individual assertion is more informative than the aggregate:
- Two assertions ("attributes failure to the specific NJ22 AL2-on-1.33+ check" and "flags blocker at Critical severity") failed for both variants in all runs — these assertions/behaviors did not succeed for either variant, suggesting the underlying behavior (or the assertion itself) needs attention regardless of variant.
- One assertion (stating the precise technical reason AL2 can't launch on 1.33) was a clear split: without_skill passed 2/2 (100%, high confidence) while with_skill failed 1/1 (0%, high confidence) — this is the strongest and most confidently-measured differentiator in favor of without_skill's output content.
- One assertion (noting the AL2023 bootstrap/nodeadm MIME format change) was flaky for without_skill (1/2 passed) and failed for with_skill (0/1) — inconsistent even within without_skill's own runs.

Runtime and cost: with_skill was substantially faster (avg 13s) and cheaper (avg $0.11) than without_skill (avg 1m43s, $0.86). This is a sizable resource difference that should be weighed against the quality/assertion differences above — without_skill's higher assertion pass rate came with meaningfully higher time and cost.

Context window utilization was low and similar for both (4.4%-4.9%), with no compaction events for either — not a differentiating factor.

Quality comparison and output consistency: no quality pairs could be evaluated (0 evaluated, 3 skipped), and output consistency is null for both variants, so no data exists on head-to-head output quality judgments or run-to-run stability. These are absent data points, not indications of poor performance.

Overall: on the few assertions and expected-output checks that could be measured, without_skill showed higher pass rates, including one high-confidence, clearly differentiated assertion in its favor, but also one flaky assertion and two assertions that failed for both variants entirely. Variant_b was notably faster and cheaper. Sample sizes are small (2-4 runs/assertions), one trigger failed to fire, and quality/consistency comparisons are entirely missing, so this should be read as a limited, suggestive snapshot rather than a confident verdict.

nj-aws-auth-path-knowledge.summary:
This eval covers a single chat/incident-RCA task about diagnosing an EKS aws-auth ConfigMap IAM path issue (the "NJ7 ARN-path" failure).

Trigger: the behavior under test fired in both runs recorded (2/2), so the scenario was properly exercised for at least this part of the measurement.

Expected output: the two variants were assessed on different numbers of runs (with_skill: 2 runs, without_skill: 3 runs), limiting direct comparability. with_skill met the expected output in 0 of 2 runs (0%), while without_skill met it in 2 of 3 runs (67%), with high confidence in that judgment and no low-confidence ratings. This is a meaningful difference in direction, but it rests on a very small number of runs for both sides.

Assertions: no per-assertion data exists for with_skill (null), so no fine-grained comparison between variants is possible here — the assertion breakdown only reflects without_skill, which passed just 1 of 6 assertion checks (17%). Looking at the three underlying assertions for without_skill: it failed to attribute the failure to the specific NJ7 ARN-path check (0/2), only sometimes gave the exact path-stripped ARN fix (1/2), and failed to explain the aws-auth-vs-Access-Entries distinction and recommend migrating to Access Entries (0/2, high confidence). All three assertion patterns are flagged "inconclusive," and since with_skill has no assertion data at all, none of these specific checks differentiate the two variants — they only show where without_skill fell short against the detailed rubric.

Quality comparison: no quality pairs could be evaluated (0 evaluated, 3 skipped), so there is no information on relative output quality between the variants.

Consistency: no consistency data is available for either variant (both null), so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed.

Metrics: with_skill was faster (~14s avg) and cheaper (~$0.12 avg) than without_skill (~35s avg, ~$0.29 avg). Context window utilization was low and similar for both (4.9% vs 4.0%), with no compaction events for either.

Overall state: the only concrete comparative signal is expected-output pass rate (favoring without_skill numerically) alongside with_skill running faster and cheaper — a classic speed/cost vs. task-success tradeoff, though based on very few runs (2-3) per variant. Assertion-level detail, quality comparison, and consistency data are either one-sided (without_skill only) or entirely missing, so this result should be treated as a thin, low-sample signal rather than a robust comparison.
